name: Triazolam (Halcion)
summary: Ultra–short-acting benzodiazepine for short-term sleep-onset insomnia. Works fast (15–30 minutes) but carries real risks: next-day impairment, memory gaps, dependence, and dangerous interactions (especially opioids and alcohol).
description: Triazolam (Halcion) is a short-acting benzodiazepine used for short-term treatment of sleep-onset insomnia—meaning trouble falling asleep. It kicks in quickly (usually within 15–30 minutes), which is the whole point, but the trade-offs are common: grogginess, dizziness, and memory problems (including anterograde amnesia). Because dependence can develop and withdrawal can be dangerous, it should be used at the lowest effective dose, for the shortest time, and never mixed with alcohol or opioids.
patient_summary: Halcion is a fast-onset sleep med for people who can’t fall asleep. It works in 15–30 minutes, so you take it right before bed (not earlier). The downside: it can cause next-day fog, dizziness, and memory gaps—and it can become habit-forming. Never combine with alcohol or opioids. If you’ve been taking it regularly, don’t stop suddenly—taper slowly to avoid withdrawal.

linked_conditions.context: Labeled for short-term treatment (generally 7–10 days) of sleep-onset insomnia. Because of dependence, next-day impairment, and memory risks, it’s usually reserved for situations where safer options haven’t worked.

contraindications: Hypersensitivity to triazolam, other benzodiazepines, or any component of the formulation
Concurrent therapy with strong CYP3A inhibitors (e.g., itraconazole, ketoconazole, nefazodone, lopinavir, ritonavir)

efficacy_response.patient_text: Triazolam is designed for one job: helping you fall asleep quickly. It’s not a great choice for staying asleep all night, and it’s not meant for long-term nightly use.

pharmacokinetics.metabolism: Extensive hepatic metabolism; CYP3A4 hydroxylation with subsequent conjugation; includes an active metabolite (alpha-hydroxytriazolam)
pharmacokinetics.excretion: Urine (~80% as metabolites; small amounts unchanged)
pharmacokinetics.food_effect: Take on an empty stomach for reliable onset; taking with or right after a meal can delay effects

sections.heading: What It's Used For
sections.text: Halcion is a fast-onset sleep medication for short-term sleep-onset insomnia—when your main problem is getting to sleep. It’s not meant to be a long-term nightly solution, and it’s not a first-choice option when safer treatments (like CBT-I) are available.
items: {link:condition:insomnia:Insomnia (sleep onset)}: Trouble falling asleep, used short-term (often 7-10 days)

sections.heading: What People Feel
sections.intro: Everyone’s nervous system has its own personality, but these are the patterns people report most often:

quotes: It hit fast. I went from wired to sleepy in like 20 minutes.
My brain finally shut up enough to fall asleep.
It felt like someone dimmed the lights in my head.

items.category: Next-Day Fog (Especially If You Don’t Get a Full Night)
quotes: I woke up groggy and kind of clumsy.
My reaction time was off the next morning.
items.note: This tends to be worse if you take it too late, don’t sleep long enough, or combine it with other sedatives.

quotes: I didn’t remember texting people after I took it.
Conversations felt like they disappeared from my brain.
I did stuff at night that I only found out about later.
items.note: Anterograde amnesia (not forming new memories after dosing) can happen, especially at higher doses or with other sedating substances.

items.category: Rebound Insomnia + ‘My Sleep Got Worse When I Stopped’
quotes: The night after stopping, I couldn’t fall asleep at all.
It worked great… until it didn’t, and then my sleep was wrecked.
Stopping suddenly made me anxious and restless at night.
items.note: Rebound insomnia and withdrawal symptoms are more likely with longer use, higher doses, and abrupt stopping.

sections.heading: How Fast It Works
sections.text: Triazolam is built for speed. That’s why it’s taken right before bedtime—and why it can cause trouble if you don’t give yourself a full sleep window.
key_points: 15-30 minutes: You start feeling the hypnotic effect

sections.heading: How Well It Works
sections.text: Triazolam can help people fall asleep faster, especially when the main issue is sleep onset. But the clinical question is never just “Does it work?” It’s “Is it worth the risks for you?” Because it can cause next-day impairment, memory effects, dependence, and rebound insomnia, it’s typically reserved for short-term, carefully selected use.

sections.heading: Critical Safety Information
sections.highlight: Never combine with opioids or alcohol. Risk of profound sedation, respiratory depression, coma, and death.
sections.black_box: Concomitant use of benzodiazepines and opioids may result in profound sedation, respiratory depression, coma, and death. Reserve concomitant prescribing for patients in whom alternative treatment options are inadequate. Limit dosages and durations to the minimum required. Follow patients for signs and symptoms of respiratory depression and sedation.
other: Abuse, misuse, and addiction risk: assess risk before prescribing and throughout treatment
Physical dependence can develop with continued use; withdrawal can be life-threatening if stopped abruptly
Next-day impairment is a real risk—especially if you don’t get a full night of sleep
Anterograde amnesia and complex sleep behaviors can occur (doing things while not fully awake, with little or no memory)
Use extreme caution (or avoid) in respiratory disease (COPD, sleep apnea) due to respiratory depression risk
Avoid in patients with depression when suicidal risk may be present, except for acute/emergency situations
patient_counseling: Do not drink alcohol while taking triazolam. Not “a little.” None.
If you’re on opioids, tell your prescriber—this combo can be fatal. If both are truly necessary, doses should be minimal and you must be monitored.
Take it only when you can commit to a full sleep window. Don’t take it and then stay up scrolling.
Don’t drive, operate machinery, or make high-stakes decisions until you know how you respond (and the next morning).
If you’ve been taking it regularly, don’t stop suddenly—taper down slowly with your clinician.
If you have a history of substance use, medication misuse, or severe depression, this medication is usually a bad fit.

sections.heading: Side Effects
sections.summary: Most common: drowsiness, dizziness, and coordination problems. Also notable: memory impairment, abnormal dreams/nightmares, mood changes, and rare-but-serious complex sleep behaviors.
plain_language_list: Memory gaps (especially for events after taking it)

common.patient_note: Sedation is the point—until it spills into the next day. Risk goes up if you don’t sleep long enough, take it too late, increase the dose, or combine it with other sedatives.
This can feel like lightheadedness, clumsiness, or delayed reaction time. It’s a fall risk—especially at night when you get up to use the bathroom.
Unsteady gait and slowed motor control can happen, particularly in older adults or anyone sensitive to sedatives.
Usually mild, but if it’s persistent, that’s a sign this may not be your medication.
Can occur during use or when stopping, especially if rebound insomnia hits.

serious: Respiratory depression (especially with opioids, alcohol, or other sedatives): slow or shallow breathing, bluish lips, unresponsiveness — MEDICAL EMERGENCY
Severe withdrawal (after continued use or abrupt stopping): agitation, tremor, sweating, vomiting, confusion, hallucinations, seizures — MEDICAL EMERGENCY
Anterograde amnesia: doing things after dosing and not remembering them later
Paradoxical reactions: agitation, aggressive behavior, irritability, mania-like symptoms
Complex sleep behaviors: sleep-walking, sleep-driving, eating, phone calls while not fully awake, often with amnesia
Hypersensitivity reactions (rare): angioedema or anaphylaxis — stop and seek urgent care

sections.heading: Critical Drug Interactions
sections.intro: Triazolam is primarily metabolized by CYP3A4. Strong inhibitors can sharply raise levels, increasing sedation, amnesia, and respiratory risk.

items.risk: Profound sedation, respiratory depression, coma, death.
items.action: Avoid when possible. If there is no alternative, keep doses and duration to the minimum, monitor closely, and educate on overdose warning signs.

items.risk: Dangerous additive CNS depression: severe sedation, blackouts, breathing suppression, death.
items.action: Absolute no-go. No alcohol while using triazolam.

items.with: Strong CYP3A inhibitors (e.g., ketoconazole, itraconazole, ritonavir, lopinavir, nefazodone)
items.risk: Major increase in triazolam exposure leading to extreme sedation, prolonged impairment, and higher overdose risk.

items.with: Other CNS depressants (sedating antihistamines, muscle relaxants, sleep meds, cannabis, barbiturates)
items.risk: More sedation, worse coordination, higher fall risk, more memory impairment.
items.action: Avoid stacking sedatives. If unavoidable, use the lowest doses and monitor for over-sedation.

items.risk: Can increase benzodiazepine levels via CYP3A4 inhibition, raising sedation and impairment risk.
items.action: Limit or avoid grapefruit products while taking triazolam.

sections.heading: Safe Discontinuation
sections.text: If you’ve used triazolam beyond short-term, stopping suddenly can trigger rebound insomnia and withdrawal. The safest move is a gradual taper—small reductions, spaced out, with support (often CBT-I) so sleep doesn’t crash and burn.
key_points: Do not abruptly stop after continued use. Withdrawal can be severe and, in some cases, life-threatening.
Rebound insomnia is common: sleep can get temporarily worse for 1-2 days after stopping, sometimes with anxiety or mood changes.
A practical taper approach: reduce by 0.125 mg every 1-2 weeks until the lowest available dose is reached, then discontinue.
If you’ve been on it long-term or you’ve failed a taper before, go slower and pair the taper with CBT-I to reduce relapse and rebound insomnia.
Intermittent (non-nightly) use can lower withdrawal risk compared to daily use, but it still carries dependence and impairment risk.

sections.heading: Dosing Information
sections.text: Triazolam is taken immediately before bedtime for sleep-onset insomnia. Use the lowest effective dose, and only when you can get a full night of sleep. It’s typically reserved for short-term use.

adult.sleep_initial: 0.125 to 0.25 mg PO once at bedtime as needed
adult.sleep_titration: If needed, may increase to 0.5 mg PO at bedtime based on response and tolerability
adult.sleep_max: 0.5 mg PO at bedtime (maximum daily dose)

sections.simple_explanation: Halcion is short-acting and fast-onset. That makes it useful for falling asleep, but it also increases the risk of next-day impairment if you take it too late or don’t sleep long enough.

sections.heading: Pregnancy, Breastfeeding, Special Groups
sections.text: Special populations need extra caution with triazolam—especially older adults, people with respiratory disease, and anyone with substance use risk. Pregnancy and breastfeeding require individualized risk-benefit decisions, with nonmedication strategies preferred when possible.
sections.pregnancy: Benzodiazepine exposure in pregnancy can be associated with fetal and neonatal risks. Late-pregnancy exposure may cause neonatal sedation (hypotonia, lethargy, respiratory depression) and/or withdrawal symptoms (irritability, tremors, feeding difficulty). Treatment for insomnia in pregnancy should be individualized, and nonpharmacologic therapy is generally preferred as first-line when available. If exposure occurs, newborn monitoring is recommended. Patients may be encouraged to enroll in the National Pregnancy Registry for Psychiatric Medications (866-961-2388).
sections.lactation: It is not known if triazolam is present in breast milk. Some benzodiazepines have case reports of infant sedation, lethargy, or weight loss. If used while breastfeeding, infants should be monitored for respiratory depression, sedation, feeding problems, or withdrawal symptoms. Some guidance suggests expressing and discarding milk during therapy and for 28 hours after the last dose to minimize potential exposure.
sections.geriatrics: Avoid use in adults 65 and older when possible. Older adults have higher risk of cognitive impairment, delirium, falls, fractures, and motor vehicle accidents with benzodiazepines. If there is a compelling reason to use it anyway, use the lowest dose: 0.125 mg PO at bedtime as needed; maximum 0.25 mg/day, with close monitoring for next-day impairment and falls.
sections.hepatic: No specific manufacturer dose adjustment is provided; use with caution because metabolism is hepatic. Start low, titrate cautiously, and monitor for over-sedation and prolonged impairment.
sections.renal: No dosage adjustment is generally needed based on available pharmacokinetic data, but use with caution in significant renal impairment and monitor for excessive sedation.

sections.heading: Clinical Monitoring
items: Respiratory status: respiratory rate and signs of breathing suppression, especially in people with COPD, sleep apnea, or any opioid/sedative co-use.
Next-day impairment: morning grogginess, slowed reaction time, driving safety, and falls—especially with nighttime awakenings.
Memory and behavior changes: amnesia, confusion, unusual behaviors at night, and any reports of complex sleep behaviors.
Mood effects: worsening depression, irritability, agitation, or paradoxical aggression—stop and reassess if this shows up.
Misuse risk: early refill requests, dose escalation, combining with alcohol/other sedatives, loss of control, or continued use despite harm.

Insomnia course: if sleep doesn’t improve within 7-10 days, reassess for underlying psychiatric/medical causes and shift toward durable treatment (CBT-I, targeted medication alternatives when appropriate).

sections.heading: Available Formulations
sections.text: Triazolam is available as an oral tablet. Because the onset is rapid, it should be taken immediately before bedtime, ideally on an empty stomach.

sections.heading: Mechanism of Action
sections.text: Triazolam is a short-acting benzodiazepine that enhances the effects of GABA at the GABA-A receptor. Think of GABA as the brain’s braking system. By boosting GABA’s inhibitory signal, triazolam reduces neuronal excitability, producing sedation and helping sleep onset.

sections.heading: Place in Treatment Algorithm
sections.text: Halcion is not a long-term insomnia plan—it’s a short-term tool. In psychiatry, insomnia is often driven by hyperarousal (anxiety, stress, trauma, mood episodes, substances, medical issues). The best durable treatment is usually CBT-I and addressing the driver. Triazolam may have a role when insomnia is severe, sleep onset is the primary problem, and safer options have failed or aren’t available—but only with strict boundaries: lowest effective dose, shortest duration, no alcohol/opioids, and a clear exit plan to avoid dependence and rebound insomnia.

seo.title: Triazolam (Halcion): Uses, Dosage, Side Effects & Withdrawal
seo.description: Halcion (triazolam) for sleep-onset insomnia: how fast it works (15–30 min), bedtime dosing (0.125–0.5 mg), next-day impairment, memory risks, dependence, dangerous opioid/alcohol interactions, and safe tapering.

editorial.reviewStatement: Content medically reviewed and verified against FDA prescribing information, APA clinical practice guidelines, and current peer-reviewed literature.

faqs.a: Triazolam is used for short-term treatment of sleep-onset insomnia—when the main problem is falling asleep. It’s not meant for long-term nightly use because it can cause dependence, rebound insomnia, and next-day impairment.
Fast. Most people feel the hypnotic effect within 15–30 minutes. That’s why you take it immediately before bed—not earlier.

The sleep effect is typically around 6–7 hours. The elimination half-life is short (about 1.5–5.5 hours), but impairment can still carry into the next morning—especially if you don’t get a full night of sleep or you’re sensitive to sedatives.

faqs.q: What’s the typical dose for insomnia?
faqs.a: Many adults start with 0.125 to 0.25 mg at bedtime as needed. If needed and tolerated, some may increase up to 0.5 mg at bedtime (maximum daily dose). The goal is always the lowest effective dose.

faqs.q: Can I take Halcion every night?
faqs.a: That’s usually a bad idea. Triazolam is typically reserved for short-term use because tolerance, dependence, and rebound insomnia can develop. If you need nightly treatment, it’s a signal to reassess the cause of insomnia and shift toward durable options like CBT-I.

It can be. Benzodiazepines carry risks of abuse, misuse, addiction, and physical dependence—especially with higher doses or longer duration. Even when taken as prescribed, dependence can develop with continued use, and withdrawal can be dangerous if you stop abruptly.

faqs.q: Can I drink alcohol with triazolam?
faqs.a: No. Alcohol plus triazolam is a dangerous combination that can cause severe sedation, blackouts, breathing suppression, coma, and death. Zero alcohol while using this medication.

faqs.q: Why is it dangerous with opioids?
faqs.a: Both opioids and benzodiazepines suppress the central nervous system. Together they can cause profound sedation and respiratory depression (you stop breathing effectively). This combination is linked to coma and death, so it should be avoided unless there’s no alternative and monitoring is in place.

Yes. Triazolam can cause anterograde amnesia—meaning you may not form memories normally after taking it. People can do things after dosing (texts, calls, eating) and later have little or no memory, especially at higher doses or when combined with other sedatives.

These are behaviors like sleep-walking, sleep-driving, cooking/eating, or making phone calls while not fully awake—often with no memory afterward. If this happens, the medication should be stopped and reassessed immediately with your prescriber.

faqs.q: How do I stop Halcion safely?
faqs.a: If you’ve been using it beyond short-term, don’t stop abruptly. A common taper approach is reducing by 0.125 mg every 1–2 weeks until the lowest dose is reached, then stopping. If you’ve been on it long-term or you’ve struggled to discontinue before, go slower and pair the taper with CBT-I to reduce rebound insomnia.

faqs.q: Is Halcion safe for older adults?
faqs.a: Generally, it’s best avoided in adults 65+ because benzodiazepines increase the risk of falls, delirium, cognitive impairment, fractures, and car accidents. If it’s used anyway, the dose should be very low (often 0.125 mg at bedtime as needed) with close monitoring.

faqs.q: What should I do if it stops working?
faqs.a: Needing more to get the same effect is a red flag for tolerance. Increasing the dose raises risks (memory issues, falls, dependence). The better move is to reassess what’s driving the insomnia and shift toward treatments that hold up long-term—especially CBT-I.
